articles.title: The Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer Everest
articles.summary: As a new film about Sherpa Tenzing Norgay is released, we visit Pen-Y-Gwryd, the Snowdonia hotel which served as British ‘base camp’ for the 1953 expedition and where the spirit of adventure lives on.
body: I n the early hours of 2 June 1953, guests at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel in the heart of Eryri (Snowdonia) were woken from their sleep by the sound of footsteps running down the corridor outside their rooms. The commotion was followed by gleeful shouting and the sound of champagne corks popping. A late-night telephone call to the hotel’s owner had moments earlier confirmed that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had successfully summited Mount Everest. It had taken two days for the news to travel from the Himalayas to London. Serendipitously, news of the historic achievement coincided with the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II later that day.

In the days and weeks that followed, the two mountaineers were feted across the front pages of newspapers around the world. Posing awkwardly for the cameras, their beaming smiles shone out of frost-burnt faces. In the decades that followed, Tenzing Norgay’s role in the expedition was increasingly marginalised – he was a Sherpa, indigenous to the area, and the load-carrying guide, while Hillary firmly planted his ice axe in the history books.
points: As a new film about Sherpa Tenzing Norgay is released, we visit Pen-Y-Gwryd, the Snowdonia hotel which served as British ‘base camp’ for the 1953 expedition and where the spirit of adventure lives on.

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with Marmite | A kitchen in Rome
articles.summary: An umami-packed dish for when you need a flavour hit in a hurry. Here is a simple, practical recipe that I trust will be useful to many who don’t have the time for lengthy kitchen preparations. Boil the spaghetti as usual, drain it, and toss it with a little butter and parmesan.
body: This is a roughly word-for-word translation of an Italian recipe for spaghetti con l’estratto di carne (spaghetti with meat extract). It is another dish from Ada Boni’s Il Talismano della Felicità (The Talisman of Happiness), which was published in English for the first time last month and, according to the food writer and editor Angela Frenda, is “still considered one of the most precise and accurate of all cookbooks”.

I was alerted to spaghetti con l’estratto di carne by the food historian and author of A Brief History of Pasta, Luca Cesari. I recently met Luca for dinner at St John in London and, over bone marrow on toast, kidneys on toast, welsh rarebit and fried tripe, we talked about many things, including recipe outrage. Spaghetti with Marmite came up as an example, and Luca pointed out that, in terms of approach, taste and spirit, it was more or less identical to Ada’s iconic and “exquisite” recipe.

articles.title: 18 again: I returned to my life in 1990. Who – and what – would I find there?
articles.summary: I doused myself in Poison perfume and made the trip back to my childhood home, friends and college. What could I learn by re-immersing myself in a world that brimmed with hope and potential? The house in which I turned 18 was full of clocks. Dark wooden things with aged faces. Every room ticked.
body: There was no escaping time. Shortly before each hour, a mechanical whir heralded the first chime. We lived in a retirement town with an elderly and conservative population, which amplified the ticking. Worthing, on the south coast of England, was known as “God’s waiting room”. Death was there in our wide, slow roads and low bungalows, the grey sea mists and blue rinses.
But I was young, and I scorned the clocks. Time was no master of mine. I answered only to love. And poetry. And fashion. And boys I liked.

At least, I think I’ve got that right. But how well does any of us remember being 18? For 17 years, we set our sights on that beacon of independence, the coruscating wonder of adulthood and all the freedom we imagine it entails. But within a few years, the day slips from view.

How did you celebrate? What did you wish for? Who did you hope to be? And if, like me, you’ve lost all memory of your 18th and need an HRT patch, creatine powder and phone alarms to recall anything, can you get it back? Over the past month, I have tried to return to April 1990 – when I became an adult – to turn back the clocks and rediscover what life was like then. And what I was like.

articles.title: You be the judge: should my husband stop looking up menus before we eat out?
articles.summary: After losing a few stone, Abdeen now likes to plan his meals ahead, but Claire says he is taking the joy out of going to restaurants. Whose argument carries more weight? You decide. • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror.
body: I love eating out. I’m lucky that I’m naturally slim and have never really had any issues with food. Abdeen, my husband of seven years, is different and has always struggled with his weight.

When I met him, he was probably four stone (25kg) heavier than he is now. He’s lost a lot of weight using the jabs and is now very conscious of putting weight back on. I’m really proud that he’s taking his health seriously, and I don’t think the jabs are an “easy way out”, but eating out with Abdeen while he was losing weight was tricky, and it’s still a bit tedious at times.

Before we go out to eat, Abdeen will look up the menus because he wants to watch his calories. His habit often ruins the surprise for me. He will download a menu and analyse his choices before we arrive, asking me: “What are you going to get?”

I don’t want to discuss a menu before we arrive at a restaurant. I like not knowing what I’m going to eat until I see another diner beside me order it, or speak to the waiting staff and think: “Ooh, that sounds nice.”
points: After losing a few stone, Abdeen now likes to plan his meals ahead, but Claire says he is taking the joy out of going to restaurants.

articles.title: The Business Case for Nature
articles.summary: As the climate crisis accelerates and geopolitical tensions disrupt fashion supply chains, executives are reckoning with relentless volatility. Could investing in nature hold the key?
body: In 2022, devastating floods left cotton farmers in Pakistan in an impossible position. As much as 40% of the annual cotton yield had been wiped out. Their livelihoods were at stake, and fashion companies like H&M that would have bought that cotton were left hanging.

The situation had a “huge impact” on H&M’s ability to get the cotton it needed at the price and time necessary, says H&M Group’s biodiversity impact lead Jennie Granström. “Now, we are scaling regenerative agriculture in cotton, and that’s primarily for resilience — so we can feel safe that there will be raw material production in a world where climate change puts a lot of pressure on nature and farmers.”

Situations like this are becoming increasingly frequent and more intense as the climate crisis accelerates. And it’s not just cotton. Fashion is vulnerable to a wide-ranging slate of nature risks, affecting everything from the quality and quantity of natural fibers to the effectiveness of dyeing and tanning processes, and the insurability of its supply chain and retail networks.
points: As the climate crisis accelerates and geopolitical tensions disrupt fashion supply chains, executives are reckoning with relentless volatility.

articles.title: Shanghai Designer Mark Gong’s Million-Dollar Moment
articles.summary: How the designer built his brand on Sex and the City’s Samantha Jones, K-pop stars, and hard work.
body: Mark Gong can remember the exact time and date when he found out that Jennie from Blackpink had been photographed in his now-famous dog print T-shirt: “It was February 24, 2025 — 3pm. That was crazy, I was freaking out.”

Anticipating a spike in demand for the cotton tee, which features six dachshunds wearing pearl necklaces, the team called up their supplier and ordered an extra 500 units. By the time the designer had returned from a barbershop appointment that same day, all pre-orders had been filled. “I was like, OK, let’s go big, let’s try 2,000,” he recalls. So, 30,000 dog T-shirt sales later, the 28-year-old designer’s business is buoyant and looking to build on the momentum.

The eponymous label — stylized as Markgong — currently employs around 17 full-time staff and six freelancers, who work across everything from pattern-cutting and embroidery to supply chain management and finance. “If you’re a designer here in China, you’re not just a designer, you’re a business person,” he says. “You have to be a boss.”
points: How the designer built his brand on Sex and the City’s Samantha Jones, K-pop stars, and hard work.

This crawl took place on a Saturday in September, filled with drinks and snacks (but mostly bites of bar burgers), working our way from Santa Monica to Manhattan Beach before wandering inland for dinner in Torrance, home to some of the best Japanese food in the United States.

The plan was to start relatively early, enjoying as much sunlit ocean breeze as we could, while also allowing me to get a normal amount of sleep at the end of the night before waking up at traditional dad hours. articles.title: Céline Dion’s Chanel Look Nods to Her 1997 Oscars Dress—and Took 1,380 Hours to Make
articles.summary: The star wore a custom Chanel gown that nodded back to her glitzy red-carpet look at the 1997 Oscars.
body: Last month, Celine Dion made her glorious return to the stage in Paris, following a years-long private battle with stiff-person syndrome (SPS). And what a return it was: The iconic French Canadian singer has been hitting the stage at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, France, exiting her hotel before each performance wearing a different high-fashion look, and then hitting the stage in similarly buzzy outfits, including custom Dior and Givenchy, among others.

This evening, however, Dion closed out her final week of shows (until May 2027, when she picks the tour back up) on an even more fabulous fashion note: The star opened her concert tonight wearing a custom Chanel dress that was inspired by the glitzy gown she wore back at the 1997 Oscars.

Back at the ’97 awards show, Dion made history when she became the first artist to perform twice during the same Oscars ceremony. (She sang her own hit “Because You Loved Me,” and a cover of Barbara Streisand’s “I Finally Found Someone.”) The star did so in a glitzy, silver plunging Chanel gown and comet-style necklace from Chanel, designed by Karl Lagerfeld, the brand’s designer at the time.

articles.title: Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants.
body: Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home.

Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads.

articles.title: On Her Upcoming Third Album, Charlotte Cardin Is Ready to Take On the World
articles.summary: The Canadian musician has already conquered France and Canada—but with the ravishing ‘Midnight, Mon Amour,’ the rest of the world should be taking notice.
body: When Charlotte Cardin appears on screen from Paris, she’s almost at the end of the fashion week whirlwind. Once upon a time, the Canadian singer-songwriter could be found on the runways herself: back in the mid-2010s, she even walked for the likes of Jacquemus and Christopher Kane. Thanks to her Jane Birkin cheekbones and statuesque height, she continues to find herself pulled into the industry’s orbit, even well over a decade into her career as a musician—this season, she took in the Saint Laurent show from the front row. Right now, however, she’s ready to focus on the music. “Mostly promo and the album announcement,” she says, smiling. “All of that fun stuff.”

After all, Cardin—who divides her life between Paris and her hometown of Montreal—is on the precipice of a new chapter. On Friday, she unveiled her slinky, retro-tinged new single, “Memories” (alongside a twin-track French counterpart, “Souvenir,” but more on that later). And more crucially, it serves as the official introduction to her ambitious third studio album, Midnight, Mon Amour, announced this week and set for release on January 29 via The Orchard and Cult Nation.
points: The Canadian musician has already conquered France and Canada—but with the ravishing ‘Midnight, Mon Amour,’ the rest of the world should be taking notice.

articles.title: The Kazakh Designers Telling Stories of Their Nomadic Heritage
articles.summary: Looking to reconnect with her Almaty origins, writer Yulia Denisyuk heads to the Kazakh capital to meet artists exploring their own identities through craft.
body: The summers I spent in Almaty form some of my sweetest childhood memories. I was born in Kazakhstan’s former capital (and still its largest city) and moved to Estonia in 1986, at age three, returning every school break into my teenage years. Once I relocated to the United States in the early 2000s, the frequent visits stopped. In my preliminary years overseas, I handled bouts of nostalgia by conjuring up those memories: eating ice cream below the mosaicked swallows of Qarlygash Cafe (which means swallow in Kazakh) near my grandmother’s apartment, or catching rare glimpses of felt-covered yurts in the foothills of the Tian Shan mountains from my grandfather’s Zhiguli sedan.

Decades in the US have since turned my Kazakh past into something distant, but as I’ve grown older—and watched my loved ones in Almaty age, too—I’ve yearned to regain a link to my origins. So this year, I returned, hoping to reconnect with the landscapes and motifs of Kazakhstan that I still hold dear, and to meet the crop of young Kazakh artists who, like me, are increasingly examining their own identities through them.
